pool.q: On which day do the optic pits appear in the developing embryo?
pool.rationale: Day 23
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q1

pool.q: On which day does the embryonic fissure close?
pool.rationale: Day 33 The optic pits first appear on day 23 of gestation (Fig. 2-8). Evagination of the optic vesicle occurs on day 25 with induction of the lens on day 28. Closure of the optic fissure occurs on day 33 (Fig. 2-9). This closure allows pressurization of the globe. The optic fissure closes on approximately day 33 of gestation. It begins midway between the optic nerve and the iris and “zips up” in both anterior and posterior directions. The fissure is located inferiorly on the globe, and corresponding inferior iris (Fig. 2-10), choroidal, and optic nerve colobomas can be seen with failure of the fissure to close properly. Lid colobomas do not occur from failure of the fetal fissure to close.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q2

pool.q: A newborn infant presents with this finding (Fig. 2-1). What developmental anomaly caused this presentation?

options.b: Faulty migration of neural crest cells

pool.rationale: Incomplete closure of embryonic fissure The patient shown has a large chorioretinal coloboma, which is due to incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure. These types of colobomas may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris. Faulty migration of neural crest cells results in anterior segment dysgenesis. A morning disc anomaly has abnormal proliferation of glial tissue. Abnormal retinal proliferation can result in retinal dysplasia.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q3

pool.q: A 2-day-old infant presents with this finding (Fig. 2-2). A developmental anomaly occurred during which stage of ocular embryogenesis?
pool.rationale: Fifth month During the sixth week of gestation, the eyelid folds begin to develop. During month 3, eyelid folds lengthen and fuse. Separation of the upper and lower lids occurs during month 5. The patient shown has anklyoblepharon, which is due to incomplete separation of the upper and lower eyelids.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q4

pool.q: This patient’s clinical presentation (Fig. 2-3) is due to an abnormality during which stage of ocular embryogenesis?
pool.rationale: Sixth week The picture shows a patient with Peters anomaly, which is due to faulty migration of neural crest cells during the sixth week of ocular development. The optic pit forms during week 3. The anterior chamber and Schlemm canal develop during months 3 and 4 of gestation.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q5

pool.q: All of the following are true regarding the embryologic development of retinal vessels, except:
pool.rationale: Grow to temporal ora by 34 weeks gestation Retinal vessels develop de novo from precursor mesenchymal tissue, beginning during gestational month 4. The vessels radiate outward from the optic nerve, reaching the nasal ora by week 32 and the temporal ora approximately 1 to 2 months later.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q6

pool.q: The following are all remnants of the hyaloidal vascular system except:
pool.rationale: Corneal leukoma Remnants of the hyaloid vasculature system include the Mittendorf dot on the posterior aspect of the lens, the Bergmeister papilla at the optic nerve head, and persistent pupillary membrane. A corneal leukoma may be seen with Peters anomaly, but this represents an abnormality in the anterior segment cleavage.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q17

pool.q: Which is true about the vitreous?

options.a: Collagen is the major structural component.
options.b: Its strongest attachments are at the vitreous base, optic nerve, and retinal vessels.
options.c: Posterior vitreous detachment results from the collapse and contraction of collagen fibers, which occurs with age.

pool.rationale: All of the above The vitreous is made up of 98% water and 0.1% colloids. The remainder of the solid matter consists of ions and low-molecular-weight solutes. The two major structural components are collagen and hyaluronic acid. Its strongest attachments are at the vitreous base (straddling the ora serrata), optic nerve, and retinal vessels. The collapse and contraction of collagen fibers, which occurs with age, causes pockets of fluid to form within the vitreous and the vitreous to reorganize and form posterior vitreous detachments (floaters).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q18

pool.q: A 10-year-old male presents with this finding (Fig. 2-4). Which of the following statements about myelination is false?

options.a: Myelination begins at the lateral geniculate body and progresses anteriorly.
options.b: Myelination begins at the lamina cribrosa and extends posteriorly.
options.c: Abnormal myelination is due to a defect in the lamina cribrosa.

pool.rationale: Myelination begins at the lamina cribrosa and extends posteriorly. The figure shows myelination of the nerve fiber layer, which is an abnormal finding due to aberrant myelination beyond the lamina cribrosa. Scientists postulate this anterior extension of myelin may be secondary to a defect in the lamina cribrosa. Myelination of the optic nerve starts in the seventh month of gestation and is usually completed 1 month after birth.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q19

pool.q: Which of the following is true of the optic canal?

options.a: It is between 8 and 10 mm in length.
options.b: It is located within the lesser wing of the sphenoid.
options.c: Sympathetic nerves pass through this canal.

pool.rationale: All of the above The optic canal contains the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and sympathetic nerves. The superior orbital fissure is separated from the optic canal by the bony optic strut. The canal ranges between 8 and 10 mm in length. It typically measures less than 6.5 mm in diameter at the optic foramen.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q20

pool.q: Which bone does not form part of the orbital floor?
pool.rationale: Lacrimal The orbital floor is composed of contributions from three bones: maxillary, zygomatic, and palatine (Fig. 2-11). The lacrimal bone is part of the medial orbital wall.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q21

pool.q: The medial wall of the orbit includes:

options.a: the ethmoid bone, the anterior ethmoidal foramen, the infraorbital foramen
options.b: the lacrimal bone, the superior orbital fissure, the zygomaticotemporal foramen
options.c: the frontoethmoidal suture line, the posterior ethmoidal foramen, the posterior lacrimal crest
options.d: the lacrimal bone, the anterior lacrimal crest, the supraorbital foramen

pool.rationale: The frontoethmoidal suture line, the posterior ethmoidal foramen, the posterior lacrimal crest The infraorbital foramen is on the anterior face of the maxilla; the zygomaticotemporal foramen is in the lateral orbital rim; the supraorbital foramen is in the frontal bone; the superior orbital fissure separates the roof and the lateral walls of the orbit.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q22

pool.q: Which one of the following statements concerning the lateral orbital tubercle is true?
pool.rationale: Attachments between the lateral rectus and the tubercle serve as a check ligament of the lateral rectus. Whitnall orbital tubercle is located entirely on the zygomatic bone approximately 2 mm inferior to the frontozygomatic suture line. Lockwood ligament acts as a suspensory system for the globe. It attaches medially to the medial orbital wall behind the posterior lacrimal crest. It attaches laterally to the lateral retinaculum, which attaches to the lateral orbital tubercle. Whitnall ligament is the superior transverse ligament that arises from the compacted sheath of the anterior portion of the levator muscle. Laterally, Whitnall ligament attaches approximately 10 mm superior to the lateral orbital tubercle to the frontal bone and to the lacrimal gland capsule. Whitnall ligament does send some extensions to the medial and lateral retinacula. The check ligament of the lateral rectus, the lateral canthal tendon, the lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis, and Lockwood ligament attach to the lateral retinaculum, which attaches to the lateral orbital tubercle.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q23

pool.q: Each rectus muscle is supplied by two to three anterior ciliary arteries, except:
pool.rationale: Lateral rectus The lateral rectus is supplied by one anterior ciliary artery.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q29

pool.q: Which one of the following statements describing the adult orbit is false?

options.a: The volume of the orbit is 30 ml.
options.b: The maximum width is 1 cm behind the anterior orbital margin.
options.c: The depth of the orbit averages 50 mm from the orbital entrance to the apex.
options.d: The medial walls are parallel and border the nasal cavity, ethmoid air cells, and sphenoid sinus posteriorly.

pool.rationale: The depth of the orbit averages 50 mm from the orbital entrance to the apex. The depth of the orbit varies from 40 to 45 mm from the orbital entrance to the orbital apex. The distance to the apex becomes important in the dissection or excision of a tumor in the posterior orbit or in the repair of an extensive blowout fracture.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q30

pool.q: Which one of the following is not a branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve?
pool.rationale: Zygomaticofacial nerve The trigeminal nerve divides into three segments: ophthalmic (V ), maxillary (V ), and, 1 2 mandibular (V ). The ophthalmic nerve is divided into three branches: nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal. The frontal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic (V ) segment, divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. The maxillary (V ) segment divides into the infraorbital, zygomatic, and superior alveolar nerves. The zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal nerves are branches of the zygomatic nerve (V ). Figure 2-13 shows the three segments of the trigeminal nerve and the various nerve branches.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q31

pool.q: Which one of the following statements about the nasolacrimal system is false?

options.a: Lacrimal sac fossa is bordered by lacrimal and maxillary bones.
options.b: Nasolacrimal sac, duct, and canaliculi are lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
options.c: Nasolacrimal duct measures 12 to 15 mm in adults.
options.d: Nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

pool.rationale: Nasolacrimal sac, duct, and canaliculi are lined by stratified squamous epithelium. The nasolacrimal system is lined with pseudostratified columnar epithelium, similar to that found in the upper respiratory system. The lacrimal sac fossa is bordered by the anterior lacrimal crest of the maxillary bone and the posterior lacrimal crest of the lacrimal bone. In adults, the canaliculi are 10 mm long (8 mm horizontal, 2 mm vertical), the nasolacrimal sac is 10 mm and the duct is 12 to 15 mm in length. The lacrimal duct extends into the inferior meatus 3 to 5 mm before opening at the membranous valve of Hasner (Fig. 2-14).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q32

pool.q: The “gray line” of the eyelid is:

options.a: the mucocutaneous junction of the eyelid margin
options.b: the location of the meibomian gland orifices

pool.rationale: The muscle of Riolan The gray line corresponds to the lid’s orbicularis muscle layer, the muscle of Riolan.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q33

pool.q: A full-thickness stab incision located 11 mm superior to the eyelid margin over the pupil in the Caucasian upper eyelid would be close to each of the following structures except:
pool.rationale: Glands of Moll A full-thickness incision in the upper eyelid 11 mm superior to the eyelid margin would involve the skin, orbicularis, orbital fat, and levator aponeurosis. The incision may also pass through the peripheral arterial arcade, the superior tarsal muscle, and the conjunctiva. The accessory glands of Wolfring are located along the orbital margin of each tarsus. The accessory lacrimal glands of Krause are located in the fornices, and most reside in the lateral part of the upper fornix. The glands of Moll would be located the farthest distance from this incision because they are located at the lid margin (Fig. 2-15).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q34

pool.q: An abnormality in which eyelid structure can cause this clinical presentation (Fig. 2-5).
pool.rationale: Periocular skin The patient shown in this figure has epiblepharon, an anatomic variation where a redundant fold of periocular skin causes inward rotation of the eyelashes, lash–corneal touch, and secondary keratitis. Epiblepharon is more common in Asian infants. It should be differentiated from ectropion and entropion, which present with outward and inward rotation of the lid margin respectively.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q35

pool.q: A 4-year-old male shown here is referred for evaluation of congenital ptosis (Fig. 2-6). Which of the following abnormal examination findings would you expect to see?
pool.rationale: Reduced levator palpebrae function A patient with congenital ptosis will present with minimal to absent levator function, often with an absent lid crease. Frontalis function is normal. An aberrant connection between CNs III and V is seen in Marcus Gunn jaw winking phenomenon. Patients with aponeurotic ptosis present with an abnormally high lid crease secondary to levator dehiscence.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q36

pool.q: Which one of the following is not a true basement membrane?
pool.rationale: Bowman membrane Bowman membrane represents a compact collagen layer at the anterior aspect of the corneal stroma (Fig. 2-16). It is not a true basement membrane.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q37

pool.q: Which structure divides the lacrimal gland into two lobes?
pool.rationale: Levator aponeurosis The lacrimal gland is split into two lobes by the lateral extent of the levator aponeurosis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q38

pool.q: Which muscle originates in the orbital apex above the annulus of Zinn?
pool.rationale: Superior oblique The superior oblique and levator palpebrae muscles originate in the orbital apex superior to the annulus. All of the recti muscles originate from the annulus of Zinn (Fig. 2-12). The inferior oblique originates behind the lacrimal fossa.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q39

pool.q: Which extraocular muscle has the shortest tendon?
pool.rationale: Inferior oblique The inferior oblique has the shortest tendon length and the superior oblique has the longest tendon.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q40

pool.q: Which muscle inserts the farthest posterior to the limbus?
pool.rationale: Superior oblique The recti muscles insert along the spiral of Tillaux with the medial rectus being the closest to the limbus (5.5 mm) and the superior rectus being the farthest (7.9 mm). The superior and inferior oblique muscles insert posterior to the equator. The superior oblique inserts on the globe in a long arc, with the anterior fibers near the insertion of the superior rectus.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q41

pool.q: The patient seen here (Fig. 2-7) presents with the most common childhood primary orbital malignancy, which is due to an abnormal proliferation of which of the following?
pool.rationale: Mesenchyme Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children. It arises from undifferentiated pluripotent mesenchymal cells, not extraocular muscle. Histiocytosis X arises from histiocytes and capillary hemangioma arises from an abnormal proliferation of vascular endothelial cells.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q42

pool.q: Which statement regarding lens structure is false?

options.a: The Y suture represents the ends of the lens fibers.
options.b: The lens nuclei are concentrated near the equator.
options.c: The lens fibers in the nucleus continue to divide throughout life.
options.d: The anterior Y suture is oriented upright.

pool.rationale: The lens fibers in the nucleus continue to divide throughout life. The lens (Fig. 2-17) is formed by the successive division and elongation of lens fibers from embryonic surface ectoderm. The nuclei are found in a lens bow near the equator of the lens. Dividing lens epithelium on the periphery continually adds fibers to the nucleus throughout life. The ends of the elongated lens fibers meet anteriorly and posteriorly, forming the Y sutures. The anterior suture is upright, whereas the posterior is inverted (Fig. 2-18).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q43

pool.q: Which statement regarding Müller cells is false?

options.a: They are modified glial cells that provide structural framework supporting neural elements in the retina.
options.b: Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer.
options.c: Their basal processes extend out to form the inner surface of the retina (inner limiting membrane).
options.d: The apical or outer cell processes extend beyond the outer nuclear layer, where they are connected to the photoreceptors by a system of terminal bars that comprise the external limiting membrane.

pool.rationale: Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer. The nuclei of the Müller cells lie in the inner nuclear layer, whereas the nuclei of the photoreceptors lie in the outer nuclear layer.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Embryology and Anatomy, Q44
